results.title: What are the advantages and disadvantages of test coverage? - Quora
results.content: What are the advantages and disadvantages of test coverage? + High numeric coverage doesn’t guarantee correctness — tests can execute code without asserting useful behavior. My rule of thumb is: strive for full coverage, but don’t test code that’s too hard. It is very possible that 100 lines of code can need 1000 lines of tests, to reach, I don't know, maybe 80% coverage. Disadvantage: it will take time to achieve good test coverage. By which I mean to say; it is not uncommon for companies that strive for near 100% code coverage to have their developers spend more time writing the unit tests than the actual code. Do we really need coverage for unit testing? Since I started writing tests first, I’ve not used coverage. Since I started writing tests first, I’ve not used coverage. results.title: Test Coverage in Ember Applications with CI and Code Climate Integration
results.content: # Test Coverage in Ember Applications with CI and Code Climate Integration. Updated Apr 10, 2025 • 5 min read. I want to show you how to set up your Ember app to automatically generate test coverage reports and send them to Code Climate. This will help you to keep track of test coverage status in your app. ## Istanbul.js with Ember - meet ember-cli-code-coverage. In our example, we’ll be using ember-cli-code-coverage which utilizes istanbul.js for Javascript test coverage calculations. $ ember install ember-cli-code-coverage. Actually, the ember-cli-code-coverage addon is **ready to run without any configuration**, but if you want/need to - you can change a few options. **Running tests with test coverage reporter is simple**, just enter the following in your project directory:. Now, if you actually have some JS code in your app (**with matching test files - so if you have my-component.js you’ll need the my-component-test.js file**), you’ll notice some new files in the /coverage folder. What interests us the most is lcov.info (which will be transferred to Code Climate later) and index.html, which contains the visual report. This gives you a quick summary of test coverage in the current scope. ## How to generate test coverage reports in CircleCI? We’ve got our test coverage reports generated locally, but what if we want to generate them in a continuous integration service, such as CircleCI? We just need to override the default test command in circle.yml:. But wait, what is this codeclimate-test-reporter stuff? Like I said at the beginning, we also want to publish our test coverage report to Code Climate. 1. Install the Code Climate addon In circle.yml in the dependencies:pre section add:. - npm install -g codeclimate-test-reporter. This will install codeclimate-test-reporter before any tests are run, and the post hook we’ve entered in test override settings will run reporter after finishing the tests. Now, you push your changes to the repo and when the tests finish, codeclimate-test-report should send the results to Code Climate:. Now, if you open your repo on Code Climate, you should notice a new badge just under the score. Now, you’ve got a test coverage tool set up along with Code Climate reporter. ## Read more on **our Blog**.

results.title: Better CI Test and Publish Stages for .NET - Code Onward
results.content: Published Time: 2023-01-10T12:30:00+00:00 Better CI Test and Publish Stages for .NET - Code Onward 3. Better Practices in CI, .NET, and GitHub Actions: CI Test and Publish Stages Better Practices in CI, .NET, and GitHub Actions: CI Test and Publish Stages * Post published:January 10, 2023 Part 1 of 3 of the Better CI In Stages series #### Portfolio Project This series covers an example for .NET CI. This post will cover the CI test and publish stages. The script has the test and publish jobs dependent on the build job. The deploy job then requires both test and publish jobs to run. We get the speed of running test and publish jobs concurrently, yet we still block the deploy if either fails. ### Test Stage Yaml name: API Black-Box Testing key: nuget-${{ hashFiles('LabDemo.MinimalApi/')}} - name: Download artifact from build job uses: actions/download-artifact@v3 # artifacts are overkill for this small of project, but done as a # poc and best practice for larger systems dotnet test $TEST_PROJECT/$TEST_PROJECT.csproj -c Release -o $BUILD_PATH ### Caching and Dependencies On line 23, did you notice that the cache is only the app’s external dependencies in the cache? We cache app dependencies for use in the build, test, and publish jobs. Both the build and nuget subdirectories growing in size after `dotnet test` built the test project ### Test Stage Summary So, the test stage uses the app dependencies from the cache and the app build output as an artifact to save time, to save from repeating steps done in the build stage. This stage requires the build artifact (generated in the build stage and used by the test stage), then generates the final product to be delivered and deployed. ### Publish Stage Yaml - name: App's nuget from cache key: nuget-app-${{ hashFiles('LabDemo.MinimalApi/')}} - name: Download artifact from build job uses: actions/download-artifact@v3 # artifacts are overkill for this small of project, but done as a # poc and best practice for larger systems run: dotnet publish $PROJECT/$PROJECT.csproj -c Release -p:OutDir=$BUILD_PATH -o $PUBLISH_PATH - name: Upload artifact for deployment uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3 ### Caching and Dependencies On line 18 of the publish job the cache is accessed, and on line 29 the download of build artifact happens.

results.content: In this blog post I will show how to display the code coverage number and HTML report if you are running end-to-end tests on GitLab CI.
